original.reason: In the converse, the proof assumes without justification that A={x_n} is infinite. More importantly, it claims T1 supplies a neighborhood of y excluding each x_i. This is impossible when x_i=y, which may occur because a limit point can belong to A. Consequently V need not avoid A, so the claimed contradiction is not established. The theorem is correct; one can instead exclude only the finitely many x_i distinct from y and obtain V∩A⊆{y}.

judgment.reason: It correctly establishes that A is infinite, but repeats the fatal converse error: if some x_i=y, no neighborhood of y can exclude x_i. Thus V need not contain no point of A, and the contradiction is not proved.
The proof of infinitude of A is adequate, but T1 cannot provide a neighborhood of y excluding x_i when x_i=y. Hence the assertion V∩A=∅ is unjustified.
The converse incorrectly excludes every x_i for i≤N from a neighborhood of y; this fails if y equals one of those points. Therefore the final contradiction does not follow as written.
Although A is properly shown infinite, the T1 argument wrongly assumes y can be separated from x_i even if x_i=y. The neighborhood may contain y, so it is not shown to avoid A.
